LINE ITEM

Therm

FIG. 01 — SCHEMATIC

Visual representation of Therm mechanics.

The Short Answer: Therm is a therm is 100,000 btu of heat energy and appears on gas bills; electric bills use kwh instead. On a commercial bill, this line typically indicates reduce therms exposure.

FIG. 02 — STRUCTURAL CONTEXT

Why Utilities Use This Model

Utilities impose this specific charge to recover the capital and operational costs of maintaining grid reliability. For reduce therms scenarios, this ensures the infrastructure can handle sudden spikes in demand without causing localized brownouts or requiring expensive emergency power purchases.

🧮 Worked Scenario

If your monthly bill is $1,000 and you used 5,000 kWh, your blended effective rate is 20¢/kWh. If this Therm increases by 10%, your total bill rises to $1,100 even if your usage stays exactly the same.

FIG. 03 — COMMON ERRORS

The Common Misread

The most common mistake is assuming gas volume is often corrected for pressure and temperature, so meter units and billed therms differ. In reality, the billing structure separates these mechanics to reflect grid realities.

How to spot this: Look on page 2 or 3 of your PDF bill under sections labeled "Detailed Charges," "Tariff Schedule," or "Riders." It may appear abbreviated (e.g., "Dem Chg" or "Fac Chg").

🎯 Your One Action This Week

Focus on reduce therms. Review your last two bills to see if this specific lever is driving your costs.
